titleStmt.title: Towards a Schedulability-driven Architecture Exploration for Mixed Criticality Multicore Systems

analytic.title: Towards a Schedulability-driven Architecture Exploration for Mixed Criticality Multicore Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Architecture space exploration of multicore systems has been studied for more than a decade now. The main exploration factor was the workload distribution in a sense that all processing elements run fairly similar workloads, and none of the processes misses its real-time constraints. For safety critical systems, assigning the software functions to real-time tasks of the target operating system is a crucial task as it is constrained with a set of different criticality, architectural and time-related constraints. Finding a suitable architecture configuration involves many important design decisions that have a strong impact on the system safety and performance. With the increasing complexity and scale of today's systems and the large number of possible architecture configurations, identifying the efficient architectures while satisfying different (potentially conflicting) criteria becomes tedious and error-prone for designers. In this paper, we propose an automated method using multi-objective criteria to explore the architecture of multicore safety critical systems. Our method relies on a constellation of analysis techniques where we consider architectural, criticality and time requirements (schedulability). We have implemented two Matlab algorithms to perform the architecture exploration, while the final candidate configurations are analyzed for schedulability using the Uppaal model checker.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the design of safety critical systems, software engineers are expected to provide an efficient association of the functions of the software application to the tasks of the execution platform. The association of functions to tasks defines a system architecture [30], [20], [28]. The early design decisions in regards to the system architecture may affect not only the performance and quality of service but would also impact the safety properties [10], [25], [18]. So that different architectures for the same software system functionality, deployed on the same hardware platform, can end up with different answers to the satisfaction of a given safety property.

One way to decide the architecture of a given system is by exploring and analyzing all potential configurations. The number of such configurations is enormous, in particular when considering multicore platform [30]. However, the number of architectures to be explored can be reduced drastically if one considers the architectural and real-time constraints, on-the-fly, when exploring the architecture space [9], [1]. Hence, only the architecture configurations satisfying the system requirements will be subject to further analysis to guarantee the safety properties. To make the the architecture design process efficient and credible, one needs to consider fine grained system models. In fact, the more fine grained the models are, the more accurate and less approximating the analysis will be.

To achieve re-usability and cost reduction, a significant trend in building large complex real-time systems is to integrate separate application modules of different criticalities in a common hardware platform. When talking about mixed criticality systems, the integration can be subject to different constraints and requirements in order to maintain safety, criticality, traceability and management. Architecture exploration of multicore systems has been intensively studied for more than a decade [18], [13], [12], [26], [22]. However, the increasing deployment of embedded systems in different application areas led to new constraints and requirements for the software architecture. Most of the modern standards dictating the architectural and safety requirements for safety critical automotive and avionic systems [31], [27] impose separation of concerns to achieve robust partitioning. Among the recent driving factors for software architecture, the functions having different levels of the security signatures may not be integrated in the same tasks [12], [16]. Besides, in avionics and automotive, functions developed by an external vendor are not very welcome to be integrated in the same task as kernel functions developed by the system owner [3]. Other exclusivity factors can be performance-driven [15], [7] where, for example, memoryintensive functions need to be fairly distributed -in an exclusive way-among tasks so a given task is not eternally stuck in memory interference [32].

On the other hand, different requirements push certain functions to be integrated within the same tasks in order to minimize the inter-task communication and shorten the tasks response time. As an example, communication functions are usually integrated within the same tasks as cryptographic protection function mechanisms [19], [23].

The architecture space exploration techniques proposed in the state of the art do not consider criticality-related constraints. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge none of the existing exploration techniques has considered the memoryrelated workload (interference) and the underlying constraints for schedulability for the validation of final architecture configurations. This paper revises the state of the art of the architecture space exploration and introduces a schedulability-driven architecture space exploration of mixed criticality multicore systems. We build fine grained system models that describe the system in terms of scheduling tasks and functions. The functions are the actual system behavior described with both computation and memory access actions. We extend the set of classic architecture constraints with criticality-and timerelated requirements, and incorporate the memory interference in the workload calculation. To perform the exploration and reduce drastically the number of final architectures, we use a technique based on randomized algorithms [17]. Given the criticality nature of the systems we consider, the final architecture configurations are further analyzed for the schedulability property using symbolic model checking.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section II states the problem and motivates our work. Relevant related work is cited in Section III. Section IV presents the formal specification of the systems we consider. Section V describes our exploration and validation technique. Section VI discuses a case study. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper.

div.head: II. MOTIVATING EXAMPLE
div.p: Before demonstrating the problem tackled in this paper, let us introduce the overall architecture of the systems we consider (Figure . 1). The top level is a set of software functions to be mapped to a set of real-time tasks. In turn, tasks are statically mapped to processing cores and scheduled locally according to the adopted scheduling policies. Processing cores can share different memory levels.

The problem we are studying here is, given a functional specification of a safety critical system, how to assign functions to tasks so as to produce the best design alternatives with regards to a set of competing architectural, criticality and real-time criteria. Each function is characterized with a set of criticality and real-time requirements such as minimum criticality level, minimum and maximum execution periodicity. Assigning functions to tasks is a non-trivial task where the impact has not been formally defined in the state of the art in regards to (1) concurrency and interleaving which could contribute in combinatorial complexity and memory interference [18]; (2) how the overall performance can be affected by the architecture [10], [8]; (3) the influence of the architecture configuration on the system schedulability and safety [20], [33]. This problem requires an extensive study and verification of the feasibility of the architecture alternatives.

Moreover, performing formal verification on all potential architecture configurations is very expensive and time consuming as the number of architecture solutions is exponential on the number of functions [29], [10]. To optimize the architecture exploration cost, one could assign to each derived architecture, satisfying real-time and architecture requirements, a cost attribute in terms of how light the workload of an architecture is. Finally, only the architecture configurations having light workload will be analyzed using expensive formal verification as they are most likely schedulable.

Let's assume a system having n functions to be mapped to m tasks running on different cores. The maximum number of architecture configurations making all tasks used is m( i=n-1 i=0 (n -i)), which can be simplified to m(n(n + 1)/2).

Hence, even for the small system described in Table I having four tasks and eight functions, the total number of system architecture configurations resulting from the mapping of functions to the four tasks is 144 1 . This number can be (drastically) decreased to 8 if one considers the requirements R1, R2 and R3 during mappings calculation. The resulting configurations are called valid configurations. This would certainly decrease We calculate an attribute called spared budget for each of the 8 valid configurations, where only configurations having a positive spared budget are subject to schedulability analysis as they are most likely schedulable. This attribute refers basically to "how far a task workload, including the effective load and an under approximation of the interference time, completes before the expiry of the task execution budget". Finally, among the 8 valid configurations only 4 configurations exhibit a positive spared budget, from which only 3 configurations succeeded the schedulability analysis. These problems motivate the automation of the architecture exploration, against an extensible set of constraints, that would help not only to make better decisions, but also to reduce the time of the design process. Figure . 2 depicts the different steps we build to reduce the architecture state space and validate the final configurations.

div.head: III. RELATED WORK
div.p: The architecture space exploration of multicore systems has been studied intensively [18], [9], [30], [13], [21], [22], [26].

Hladik et al [14] use constraint programming to perform the allocation of a system workload, given in terms periodic tasks, to a set of distributed processors. Tasks are, in turn, given as sequence of instructions. The problem tackled is slightly different from ours as instructions are abstract and the mapping is calculated for task-to-processor rather than function-to-task. In a similar way, SMT solvers have been used to deduce the architecture configurations satisfying a set of criteria [11], [26], [14]. However such techniques do scale to a certain limit then diverge rapidly [11].

Li et al [18] propose a technique to find feasible mappings of synchronous programs on two types of time-predictable multicore systems. The proposal considers reaction time as a unique requirement for the design space exploration. Our work devises also a mapping of functionality into a multicore platform, but our approach departs from a set of specified functions instead of synchronous programs. Moreover, our approach considers a larger set of architecture and time-related requirements, and combines a constellation of low cost and model checking analysis processes.

In [21], the authors present a multi-objective algorithm to address the communication scheduling and the allocation of tasks in space and time to a multiprocessor architecture. Authors offer also the possibility to consider the physical platform where the type/number of processors and communication topology may vary.

In [13], the authors consider a combination of analytical and simulation tools to perform the exploration and analysis of time critical system architectures. They rely on constraint programming and an execution simulation environment to find better solutions, in the process of exploring the design space, satisfying a set of constraints.

The authors of [5], [6] consider a steady architecture where system functions are statically mapped to tasks. The configuration then is to tune the tasks inter-arrival time and study the schedulability of the resulting workload. In a similar way, the authors of [24] develop an architecture for scheduling mixed criticality real-time workloads on multiprocessor platforms where the functionality is statically allocated to different tasks, and the ultimate goal is to distribute the slack time2 among tasks to achieve an efficient resource utilization.

Butko et al [9] report on the use of simulation as a vehicle to perform architecture space exploration of many-core onchip systems. The authors develop a model of an octa-core processor in a computer-system architecture simulator. They explore the design space using the developed model by varying hardware parameters as memory and cache-size. Such casestudies provide arguments in favor of approaches where the the design process is based on an abstract description of the reference/target implementation.

Mehiaoui et al [22] introduce a 2-step optimization for the allocation of atomic communicating functions, to a set of tasks on distributed nodes, using genetic algorithms and linear programming. Our set up is similar to the one proposed in [22], except that we consider non atomic preemptible functions communicating via shared memories and we use formal verification to validate the final architecture configurations.

This paper introduces an automation for the architecture exploration and validation of mixed criticality multicore systems. We combine randomized algorithms, which is an efficient exploration, with a low-cost load calculation algorithm to derive valid architecture configurations. Such candidate architectures will then be analyzed using model checking for the schedulability property. Our architecture exploration and validation technique maintains the completeness property [14], where if a system has no feasible architecture mapping our analysis is able to demonstrate it.

div.head: IV. FORMAL SETTINGS
div.p: This section specifies the architecture and behavior of the systems we consider. Basically, a multicore real-time system is given by a set of functions abstracting the behavior of the software application processes. Such functions are mapped, according to a given architecture configuration, to a set of tasks which are in turn statically mapped to different processing cores, as depicted in Figure . 1. The objectives of this work are the following:
• Automation of the architecture space exploration for multicore systems with shared memories. • High fidelity system model describing the behavior with both computation and memory access actions.
• Efficient and scalable analysis and formal validation of the final architecture configurations. a) Assumptions.: We consider the following assumptions:
• Tasks are periodic and preemptible.
• Tasks are statically mapped to processing cores.
• Processing cores are homogeneous and run always at the same processing frequency. b) Notations.: We introduce the following notations:
• We use F to refer to the set of the system functions. F i is a subset of F and f states a single function.
• We use T to refer to the set of the system tasks. T i is a subset of T and T states a single task.
..} to refer to the set of homogeneous processing cores.

div.head: A. Software System Specification
div.p: This section describes the top layer of the system displayed in Figure . 1. A software system is given by a set of functions f 1 , f 2 , . . . , f n . Each function has an associated execution budget, a memory budget, and a set of requirements.

We consider 2 attributes α c and α m where α c corresponds to the maximum number of successful access requests (hits) to L2; α m is the number of DRAM access requests (corresponds to L2 miss) performed by a given function. Moreover, in order to distinguish between read and write accesses to each shared memory, we denote each of the attributes with r for read and w for write, i.e. α r c , α w c , α r m and α w m . A component (taskset) T = {T 1 , .., T n } is a set of periodic tasks each of which describes the execution of a real-time process for both processing and memory accesses.

div.head: Definition 1 (Memory access requests
div.p: ). An access request to a shared memory is given by req = a, RW, ψ where:
• a ∈ {L2, DRAM } is an access pattern stating to which memory the request hits.
• RW indicates whether it is a read (r) or write (w) action.

• As requests are non deterministically triggered during runtime, we use ψ to store the issue time of each request. This attribute is initially empty and will be initialized by a core when the access request is effectively issued.

ψ will be used as a ground by the FR-FCFS scheduler [8] of DRAM memory to arbitrate the concurrent access requests. For the sake of notation, we use α r c and α w c , respectively α r m and α w m , at function level as numbers of read and write accesses to L2, respectively DRAM. Implicitly, each access request to L2 is preceded by an access to the core local cache. The access requests of a given task are performed sequentially following the order they are given in.

Definition 2 (Software functions). A software function f i is given by e i , α r c i , α w c i , α r mi , α w mi where: • e i is the pure execution time of the function, i.e. e i does not include the time to fetch data from shared memories. • α r c , α w c , α r m and α w m are the number of access requests described earlier.

a) Architectural requirements.: The architecture requirements we consider are related to the criticality feature. Such requirements dictate, for a given function, the minimum criticality level of the task holding the function execution, and whether the function can share a local scope (task space) with certain functions or not. This is to maintain the separation between the criticality levels and enforce fault containment. Formally, we introduce the following functions:

• Crit : F → N defines the criticality level for any given function. For the sake of simplicity we consider criticality levels as natural numbers where a smaller number refers to a lower criticality. • Scope : F * F → BOOLEAN determines for any given pair of functions (f i , f j ) whether f i can share the same task with f j or not. If two functions (f i , f j ) are not allowed to share the same task, then Scope(f i , f j ) = f alse. The function Scope() is symmetric. Function Scope() can implement also the harmonic rate constraint [22] where functions having different period rates are prevent to be assigned to the same task.

b) Time requirements.: This set of requirements dictate time-related constraints such as minimum and maximum time intervals between two releases of a function execution. Formally, time requirements of functions are given by the function F req l : F → R ≥0 , respectively F req h : F → R ≥0 , stating the minimum period, respectively maximum period, of the task that can hold the execution of a given software function f i .

The processor time is also an implicit constraint where, for a feasible architecture configuration, the workload generated by the allocation of functions to a task must not exceed the processor budget to be supplied to that task i.e. the task worst case execution time. Besides the aforementioned constraints, one can consider inter-function communication as another constraint where functions communicating with each others are preferably to be mapped to the same task. This is in fact a recommendation to reduce inter-task communication and improve the system performance.

div.head: B. Platform Specification
div.p: We do not distinguish the operating system (RTOS) description from the platform description. RTOS is given by a set of tasks grouped in different tasksets (components), core schedulers and memory schedulers. The tasks of a component are scheduled according to the scheduling policy adopted by the processing core the taskset is allocated to. Definition 3 (Task structure). A task T is given by p, τ, d, ρ, β where:
• p is the task period.
• τ is the maximum execution time that can be allocated by RTOS to the task. • d is the relative deadline, ρ is the priority level associated to T and β is the actual task behavior.
The task behavior is accordingly given as follows:
Definition 4 (Task behavior). A task behavior β = L, l 0 , L A , → is a transition system specifying the sequence of functions performed by that task.
• L is a set of locations and l 0 ∈ L is the initial location,
• L A ⊆ L is a set of final (acceptance) locations,
• →⊆ L\L A × F × L is the transition relation leading from a non terminal location to another location through the execution of functions.

The task behavior is subject to a set of time constraints, which are the classic scheduling parameters such as period, deadline and priority. We constrain the behavior of tasks as described in Definition. 3.3.

Besides the aforementioned explicit requirements, implicit requirements considered in this paper are: 1) each function must be exactly allocated to one task; 2) the allocation of a function to a task must not exceed the processor budget of the task; 3) the resulting workload of a given task must not violate the task deadline.

As mentioned earlier, the taskset T is split into different disjoint tasksets each of which is statically allocated to a processing core. For a a given core C i , the scheduling function Φ i : T i × T i × R ≥0 → T i ∪ {none} identifies which of the tasks has priority to be scheduled at any point in time. This can be achieved through a series of pair-wise comparisons. The scheduling of a task may imply the preemption of another task. In case none of the tasks is ready, Φ returns none. Function Φ is described abstractly so that it can be instantiated for both static and dynamic priority scheduling algorithms. The scheduling policies implemented in our framework are: Firstin First-out (FIFO), Fixed Priority Scheduling (FPS) and Rate Monotonic (RM), however other scheduling policies can be implemented in a similar way.

div.head: Definition 5 (Processing cores). A core C
div.formula: i = T i , Φ, h, h c , h m , {f ree, occupied}, f ree, ∅, → C
div.p: is given by:
• T i is the set of tasks allocated to C i .

• Φ is the scheduling policy (core scheduler) adopted to arbitrate T i . • h, h c and h m are the effective time durations to access the local cache (L1), shared cache (L2) and DRAM respectively, regardless of whether the access hits or misses.

• The behavior of a processing core is a transition system consisting of two locations free and occupied, initially at location free, and a transition relation between both locations with silent labels (internal actions).

Each processing core is equipped with a local cache. For the sake of simplicity, we consider one L2 cache space only thus each core shares the L2 cache and DRAM with all the other cores. We assume that processing cores are not preemptible during data fetching, i.e. while waiting for an access to be granted. This is in fact to reduce the memory interference so that a given core does not apply the same access request twice.
The problem we are studying3 can then be formally expressed as follows:

div.p: This section shows how the architecture space is explored through the three-staged analysis chain (Figure . 2). The outcome of each analysis step represents an input to the next step. The final output of the exploration and analysis is a set of schedulable architecture configurations satisfying all the architectural and time requirements introduced in Section. IV-A.
Definition 6 (Architecture configuration). An architecture configuration M ⊆ T × 2 F is a mapping stating the set of functions allocated to each task.

For the sake of notation, we write M(T ) = {f 1 , f x , f y } for a configuration M where functions {f 1 , f x , f y } are mapped to task T . One can see that our mapping definition is similar to that of [14], given by T i → A(T i ) = C j , but differs in the level of granularity where we calculate the mapping of functions to tasks, and consider a static mapping of tasks to cores.

div.head: A. Calculation of Architecture Configurations
div.p: To calculate the architecture configurations, we iterate on the set of functions and try to map each function to the earliest task satisfying the function requirements. To achieve that, we need to check that the requirements dictated by Crit, Scope, F req l and F req h for each function will be satisfied if the function is mapped to that task, while making sure that the function load will not lead the current task load to exceed its execution budget τ . The architecture configurations resulting from this exploration step are said to be valid. For each configuration M k , we define the following functions:
div.formula: allocated(f i , T j ) = true if f i ∈ M k (T j ) f alse otherwise
div.p: We omit including M k as a parameter for allocated() as the function is going to be reset for each new configuration. Implicitly, function allocated() maintains the partitioning constraint [22] dictating that a function is exactly allocated to one task, i.e
The load of a function is its execution time, i.e. load(f i ) = e i . In a similar way, we define the load of a task by:
div.formula: load(T j ) = fi∈M k (Tj ) load(f i )
div.p: One can see that the calculation of tasks load is an underestimation as it does not include the memory access time (interference time), resulting from the cores competition to access shared memories. Memory interference can be examined using online analysis at the core level [8]. Our architecture space exploration has been implemented as a randomized algorithm in Matlab, and a sketch of it is depicted in Algorithm. 1.

The algorithm generates a set of architectures, initially an empty set (line 1). The generation works by searching the possible architecture space trying to match a sequence of functions to a sequence of tasks using a first fit approach. We assume each try is uniquely defined, and is indexed by a seed index si (line 1). We rely on an operation seed which builds the sequence of functions, and the sequence of tasks that will be iterated in the si try (line 1). The seed operation makes use of random decisions to avoid the exploration of the entire state space when the number of functions n and tasks m invalidates a brute-force approach, yet for smaller values randomness may be dropped and an exhaustive search is performed instead.

For each try an empty configuration mapping is declared (lines 1 to 1), and functions are mapped to tasks on a first fit basis. For that, the algorithm performs a sequential search for an allocation for each function f i (line 1) following the indices chosen for this try. The search works by incrementing the task's index until a solution is found, or the end of the taskset is reached. The latter case means no valid allocation is possible, as the function does not fit any task for the current try. In that case, the try is discarded by breaking the try (line 1). When a potentially different configuration is generated, the new configuration is stored in the variable Conf ig, which keeps track of the valid architectures (line 1) and a new iteration starts.
Property (Valid architecture configurations). An architecture configuration M is valid if ∀T i ∀f j ∈ M(T i ):

div.head: B. Calculation of Spared Budgets
div.p: This analysis step discards, among the set of valid architecture configurations obtained using Algorithm. 1, the configurations having high workloads. What we mean by a high workload is that the resulting load of a task converges to, or exceeds, the maximum execution time τ of the given task. Thus, there is no space in the task execution for memory interference delays. Such configurations are not schedulable due to the fact that memory interference is a strong intrinsic bottleneck in multicore systems. We define the memory access time of a function as follows:

The time remaining from the task execution τ after deducing the task workload and interference is called a spared budget. For a given configuration M k , the spared budget of each task T i is calculated as follows:

The configurations having at least one task consuming the entire execution budget (spare(T i ) ≤ 0) are immediately discarded because they are not schedulable. To optimize our framework, we compare the spared budgets of the remaining configurations and only configurations having high positive budgets will be analyzed in the next analysis phase as they are most likely schedulable. The spared budget of a configuration is calculated as follows:
div.formula: spare(M k ) = ( |T | i=1 (spare(T i )/T i .τ ))/ | T |
div.p: The obtained spare(M k ) are sorted in a decreasing order, so that the next analysis step starts the schedulability verification with the configuration having the highest spare value. If such a configuration is not schedulable then we move to the configuration having the next lower spare value.
Property (Most-likely schedulable architecture configurations). An architecture configuration M k is said to be most likely schedulable if it is a valid configuration, and ∀T i spare(T i ) > 0.
A sketch of the spared budget calculation algorithm is depicted in Algorithm. 2. The algorithm is simple thanks to the aforementioned load calculation functions.

div.head: C. Formal Verification of Schedulability
div.p: The system executions are given by the sequence of transitions where tasks compete for the cores they are allocated to, in turn the processing cores compete for the access to shared memories. This analysis step consists in analyzing all execution paths and checks whether a task runtime can reach the deadline instant whereas the task did not reach an acceptance state yet [4]. If so, a deadline miss is reported and the configuration is excluded.

Technically, the model checker explores the state space of a most-likely schedulable configuration and checks for a deadline miss. The state space is the parallel composition of processes representing tasks workload, processing cores, core schedulers and shared memories. Each state includes the status of each process, and can be a preemption point. Given that memory interference is strongly dependent to the issue time of access requests, which has a direct impact on the tasks response time, one needs to check the resulting task response times (the instant to reach an acceptance state) for all potential access request issue instants. By making memory access requests non-deterministic we have provided the model checker the ability to explore the entire state space for all arrival instants of the memory access requests. The schedulability property is expressed by the following property:
Property (Schedulable architecture configurations). An architecture configuration M k is said to be schedulable if it is a valid configuration, and for any task T i , time
div.formula: (T i ) = T i .d ⇒ loc(T i ) ∈ T i .L A .
div.p: time(T i ) and loc(T i ) are variables to track the current location and time of tasks for each period.

div.head: D. Uppaal Mechanization
div.p: We have mechanized our framework using UPPAAL [2] to perform the formal analysis phase using symbolic model checking. The system model is built in a modular way where the mapping of software functions to tasks is given as a system parameter. This makes our models easily reconfigurable in a way that uploading a new configuration to the tool can simply be achieved by updating the mapping parameters given that the characteristics of functions and tasks are the same for a given system. In the following we depict the important processes, mainly task and processing core templates.

We have implemented our task model, including behavior and constraints, by the Uppaal template depicted in Figure . 3. In fact, the task template is designed to be parameterized so that it can be instantiated for a large set of tasks. We assign an identifier to each task to ease the mapping of functions to tasks, so that a function is assigned to a task just by referring to its identifier. One can see that the template allows a task to be preempted only between 2 functions (at location Run). When the execution of a timed function is released the task moves to location FunExec where it cannot be preempted. Once the execution of a timed function completes the task moves back to location Run. The acceptance locations of the task behavior are modeled by location ExecDone, whereas the termination condition is given by the entire execution of the task workload (curFun>=task[tId].numberFuns) and the non-violation of the tasks deadline, i.e. curTime[tId]<=task [tId].deadline.

The processing core template is depicted in Figure . 4. The model is simple and consists in loading the functions of a scheduled task sequentially. Whenever a function issues an access request, non-deterministically, the processing core determines to which shared memory (DRAM or shared cache) the request is targeting so that it gets stored in the appropriate queue. Once an access request is completed the function resumes its execution unless the parent task is preempted. The tasks allocated to a given processing core are scheduled using the scheduler model depicted in Figure . 5. Roughly speaking, the scheduler of a given processing core receives execution requests from the ready tasks allocated to that core and decides which task to execute, according to the adopted scheduling policy.

div.head: VI. CASE STUDY
div.p: To show the applicability of our framework, we have analyzed a realistic example from the automotive domain (Table II). Besides the functions shown in Table. II, the system includes a duplication of the same set of functions as a backup for faults recovery. Making thus the total number of functions 16. Such functions are given with a set of criticality-and time-constraints as shown in the same Table . The architecture exploration consists in finding an allocation of the given functions to the task set (Task1, Task2, Task3, Task4) running on two identical processing cores. The data related to memory access is synthetically estimated from the number of input/output of each function. For the Scope constraint, we only stated the cases having false value, i.e. the case where functions cannot share the same task.

The first analysis step amounts at finding all potential architecture configurations, so-called valid configurations, satisfying the criticality-and architecture-related constraints. Using the set of valid architecture configurations as input, the second analysis step determines the configurations having a potentially feasible workload, i.e. so called most-likely schedulable. The mapping of each most-likely schedulable configuration is thereafter used as a parameter to our Uppaal model where the schedulability is then formally analyzed using the Uppaal model checker. The third analysis step terminates whenever there is a schedulable configuration or there is no more configurations to be analyzed, and the system is reported to be not feasible.

When analyzing this case study, we realized that the second analysis step (spared budget process) eliminates 83% of the number of valid architecture configurations to be checked. Thus, only 17% of the total architecture configurations are determined to be most-likely schedulable. This is due to the fact that the system is memory-intensive, thus the enormous number of memory accesses and the resulting interference make the majority of valid architecture configurations not "most-likely schedulable".

To study the scalability of our framework, we have generated different synthetic task sets by duplicating the tasks and functions. While maintaining the number of functions per task to 10, we vary the number of tasks and analyze the system accordingly to obtain a schedulable architecture. Figure . 6 depicts the analysis time.

By increasing the number of tasks, and functions accordingly, and maintaining the number of cores constant, the number of (non-schedulable) architecture configurations discarded at the second analysis phase increases exponentially. Thus, the third analysis phase will be applied for lesser configurations when the number of tasks reaches 16. Model checking is the most time consuming analysis phase. The time analysis trend starts converging after 20 tasks. The analysis results show that our framework scales easily for medium size systems.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper introduced a technique to explore and optimize the architecture of multicore time-critical systems with shared memories. We have built fine grained models for software functions and execution platforms. Our proposal uses a constellation of analysis techniques to explore the architecture state space and validate the final architecture candidates. The exploration has been achieved through three analysis phases following different constraints: architecture, criticality, timerelated and utilization. The number of architecture configurations to be analyzed is reduced from a phase to another by discarding the configurations not satisfying one of the constraints. The final architecture configurations are proved to be schedulable using the UPPAAL model checker.
As a future work, we intend to incorporate more realistic constraints such communication between functions and memory bandwidth.
